source.title: The Model Shape Behind Scaling Laws: A Gradient Superposition Perspective
source.authors: Wen-Jie Sun; Jin-Ning Yang; Shuai Zhang; Meng-Nan Du

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses feature superposition as motivation but does not test whether sparse features are represented by overlapping, nearly orthogonal feature directions. Its experiments measure an end-to-end input-gradient observable and its association with loss, which the authors distinguish from semantic feature overlap.
record.gate_note: The paper describes superposition and polysemanticity in related work, but does not measure feature directions, feature sparsity or importance, neuron polysemanticity, feature recovery by SAEs, or feature dimensionality. The results below concern gradient-response geometry and loss; they are recorded as related findings, not as tests of the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The paper uses superposition only as motivation. It reproduces the tied-autoencoder double-descent setup (Henighan et al. 2023), but it measures only end-to-end input AGOP norm and loss, not feature-direction geometry, sparsity-dependent transitions, neuron polysemanticity, SAE recovery or feature dimensionality. The authors state that F 'is a functional observable rather than a count of semantic features' and that the scalar does not identify semantic feature overlap. No result bears on V1–V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is essentially right. The authors conclude that input AGOP norm tracks loss in the toy double-descent sweep and among validation-selected LM shapes, and they explain the link as error-response amplification. That mechanism is proven in regression but is only an interpretation for LMs. They also state that F does not identify semantic feature overlap, and they offer a functional account of depth-width allocation (d* ∝ P^0.46).
record.recipe_differences: The toy autoencoder is used in a related double-descent setup, but the paper measures end-to-end/input AGOP and loss rather than testing the original feature-direction superposition geometry. It also studies Gaussian regression and byte-level Transformer shape scans.
record.method_sensitivity: The language-model loss–F association is regime-dependent: within-budget raw-F Pearson correlations are weak or negative at 1M and 1.6M and at least 0.95 from 10M through 50M. The paper also reports that coordinate choice, normalization, sample count, and response measure can affect AGOP or response comparisons.

fits_no_version.finding: In the tied sparse autoencoder sweep (D = 1000, bottleneck 2), test loss and input AGOP norm share a peak at n = 500 (r = 0.9789). A training-mean predictor beats the network at large n (0.992437 vs 0.993247).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the toy double-descent superposition setup, end-to-end input-gradient sensitivity tracks reconstruction loss. The late-regime network does not beat a constant baseline, which limits feature-learning readings of the second descent.

fits_no_version.finding: In noisy minimum-norm regression, risk and AGOP norm share a fitted-noise amplification term and an interpolation singularity. Both are absent without noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Risk and input-gradient norm share a fitted-noise amplification term in ridgeless regression.

fits_no_version.finding: In byte-level Transformer shape scans, test CE and normalized AGOP norm are strongly associated on the validation frontier and within budgets from 10M to 50M. The association is weak or negative at 1M and 1.6M.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The loss–AGOP association across depth-width shapes depends on the parameter-budget regime.

record.problems: The results do not measure feature-level geometry or semantic feature overlap. The sparse-reconstruction sweep uses one stated feature activity probability, and initialization SEM does not capture dataset-resampling uncertainty. The LM scan covers byte-level models up to 50M parameters, one source corpus, and unmatched compute/depth-specific tuning; its proposed error-amplification mechanism is not directly identified in those models. The authors also report estimator and coordinate dependence.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for every Gaussian-regression sample size or every local-curvature checkpoint/control: those measurements concern the paper's response-amplification and estimator audits rather than any listed feature-superposition version. Main findings, the noiseless control, aggregate LM findings, and every separately reported within-budget raw-F correlation are retained.

untested.parts: Feature-direction overlap (W^T W), near-orthogonality, regular geometry and the sparsity-dependent transition. Only one sparsity setting (p = 0.01) was used, and W^T W geometry was not reported.
Capacity competition and dedicated dimensions for important features.
Feature spreading across neurons in LLMs and SAE recovery. The byte-level Transformers were analysed only through the AGOP norm.
Completeness, stability or canonicity of SAE features.

missing.what: Matched constant-baseline comparison in the toy autoencoder: from n = 1946 onward every network is worse than the training-mean predictor. This bears on interpreting the second descent, but is not a superposition-version test.

record.verdict_notes: The title uses 'gradient superposition', which is the authors' redefinition as end-to-end response overlap, not representational superposition of features. The Henighan et al. double-descent setup is reproduced, but feature geometry is not reported, so it cannot serve as a V1 replication.

versions.untested_parts: Feature-direction overlap, near-orthogonality, regular geometry, and how the geometry changes with feature sparsity or importance.
Whether feature competition for capacity explains neuron polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemanticity arises for reasons other than capacity pressure.
Feature distribution across neurons in LLMs and recovery of sparse features with dictionaries or SAEs.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units of model representation.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: tied ReLU autoencoder
rows.operation_detail: Measured input AGOP Frobenius norm F and test reconstruction loss across the sparse-reconstruction training-size sweep.
rows.measure: Configuration-mean Pearson correlation between F and test reconstruction loss; shared peak across the sweep
rows.uncertainty: Initialization SEM is shown; the text says it does not measure data-resampling uncertainty.
rows.locator: Section 3.1, Figure 1(a), Equation (4); Appendix G, Table 4
rows.note: This measures loss–AGOP association at one stated sparsity setting, not feature-direction geometry. The authors caution that the shared peak is not identified as exact interpolation and that the late decline in F does not establish input-dependent shared-feature learning.

rows.subject: Gaussian minimum-norm regression
rows.operation_detail: Measured clean population risk and predictor AGOP norm across a sample-size sweep with noisy training targets.

conditions.value: 10 sizes; n/p spans the plotted sweep

rows.measure: Joint trajectory and interpolation peak of clean risk R and AGOP norm F
rows.value: Risk and F rise together near n = p and decline as inverse-spectrum amplification weakens; Figure 1(b) reports medians and 10–90% intervals.
rows.locator: Section 3.2–3.3, Figure 1(b); Appendix B.3, Figure 3 and Table 2
rows.note: This is a regression response-amplification result, not a test of sparse feature superposition.

rows.subject: Gaussian minimum-norm regression
rows.operation_detail: Compared clean risk and AGOP norm across the sample-size sweep with no training noise.
rows.measure: Clean risk R and AGOP norm F
rows.value: For n < p, R = S − F; the noise-driven interpolation singularity is absent.
rows.uncertainty: Medians over 128 paired repetitions are tabulated.
rows.locator: Section 3.3; Appendix B.3, Figure 3 and Table 2
rows.note: A stated control for the noise-amplification account; not a test of feature superposition.
rows.check: 'reversed' is not meaningful for any claim version. This noiseless control shows that the risk–F singularity is absent (R = S − F for n < p); it is a control for the regression mechanism, not a superposition measurement.

rows.subject: 152 byte-level Transformer configuration means (254 checkpoints)
rows.operation_detail: Measured test cross-entropy and normalized input AGOP Frobenius norm across the validation-selected shape at each budget.

conditions.value: lowest seed-mean selection-validation CE at each budget
test CE and normalized input AGOP F

rows.measure: Association between test CE and F across the twelve validation-selected frontier points
rows.value: Pearson r = 0.9733; Spearman ρ = 1.000. Descriptive fit: Ltest(F) = 0.9839 + 0.1734(F/1000)^0.5929, R2 = 0.9448.
rows.note: Aggregate over twelve selected configurations. The paper says this is a descriptive frontier, not a universal scaling law in F.
